title: From Chicago's Michelin List to Hudson Yards: Indienne Brings Progressive Indian Fine Dining to New York
excerpt: Chef Sujan Sarkar's tasting-menu restaurant, which earned a Michelin star within its first year in Chicago, has opened a 34-seat outpost in Manhattan with $195 nine-course menus that reimagine chaat and regional Indian flavors.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Indienne New York offers a $195 nine-course tasting menu reimagining Indian street food.
  • Chef Sujan Sarkar earned a Michelin star for Indienne Chicago within its first year.
  • The restaurant features a curated wine list with 100 selections, enhancing the dining experience.
  • Indienne's opening reflects a growing trend of Indian fine dining in America.
  • Sarkar plans to expand his culinary concepts further across the United States.

When Sujan Sarkar opened Indienne in Chicago's River North neighbourhood in 2022, the Kolkata-born chef had a singular ambition: to prove that Indian cuisine belonged not just on Michelin's radar but at the very top of America's fine-dining conversation. Within a year, the restaurant had its star. Now, Sarkar has brought that vision to New York City — and the stakes have never been higher. Indienne New York opened on May 28 inside Henry Hall, a luxury residential tower in Hudson Yards, with just 34 seats and a menu that reads like a love letter to Indian street food reimagined for the world's most discerning palates. ## The Menu: Chaat Meets Haute Cuisine The restaurant offers three nine-course tasting menus — a standard option at $195 per person, and vegetarian and vegan versions at $175 each. An optional wine pairing runs $125. The meal begins where all great Indian feasts do: with chaat. But these are not the pani puri you remember from Delhi's Chandni Chowk. Sarkar's signature opener is an "oyster" pani puri — a riff on the crunchy street snack featuring green mango, passion fruit, cucumber and avocado, housed in a delicate crisp shell. From there, the courses progress through seasonal plates that emphasise texture and layered spice, including a paneer kofta with summer squash and pistachio that draws on traditional North Indian technique while feeling entirely contemporary. "While select courses draw inspiration from Indienne's Chicago flagship, they have been reimagined in New York," the restaurant noted. Every dish reflects Sarkar's philosophy of blending traditional Indian flavors with European techniques — a sensibility honed across two decades of cooking in kitchens from Kolkata to London to Los Angeles. > **"Sarkar's signature opener is an "oyster" pani puri — a riff on the crunchy street snack featuring green mango, passion fruit, cucumber and avocado, housed in a delicate crisp shell."** ## A Wine Program Built for Spice Unlike many Indian restaurants where the beverage program is an afterthought, Indienne has made wine integral to the experience. The list, curated by beverage director Chris Farrell and New York cellar lead Christian DiNello, runs about 100 selections with a focus on small-production, sustainability-driven winemakers. German Riesling anchors the program — its natural acidity and subtle residual sugar offering both contrast and balance to spice-driven dishes. The cellar also stocks rare bottles, including Domaine de la Romanée-Conti Romanée-Saint-Vivant 'Marey-Monge' 2023. ![River North — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/84/Chicago_River_6.jpg/3840px-Chicago_River_6.jpg) One pairing the team is particularly excited about matches yogurt chaat with Kir-Yianni "Akakies" 2024 sparkling rosé from Greece. "The crunchy red fruit flavors and high-toned red floral qualities in the wine highlight the strawberry and tamarind hidden in the dish," Farrell and DiNello explained. ## The Bigger Picture: Indian Cuisine's Fine-Dining Moment Indienne's New York arrival comes amid an unprecedented surge for Indian fine dining in America. Three Indian chefs — Vijaya Kumar of Semma in New York, Chetan Shetty of Raina in Washington DC, and Sujan Sarkar himself at Indienne Chicago — currently hold Michelin stars. The James Beard Foundation's 2026 finalist list included Indian restaurants in multiple categories, from Srijith Gopinathan and Ayesha Thapar's Cal-India Collective in the Bay Area to the Iranis' beloved Chai Pani in Asheville, North Carolina.

Sarkar's move to Hudson Yards — one of Manhattan's most high-profile dining destinations — signals that Indian cuisine is no longer just earning critical respect; it is competing directly with French, Japanese and Italian establishments for the city's most affluent diners. ## What It Means for the Diaspora For NRIs who grew up watching Indian food relegated to the "ethnic" category in American dining, Indienne represents something profound. This is not fusion or apology cooking. It is unapologetically Indian food — chaat, kofta, biryani-adjacent rice courses — presented with the same rigour and ambition as any three-star French kitchen. Indienne New York is the first of three concepts Sarkar plans to introduce at Henry Hall, with the 3,200-square-foot space designed by Mapa Mueller to feel intimate and artful — burgundy tones, sculptural lighting and Holi-inspired paintings by Chicago artist Ken Andjulis. ## What's Next
Sujan Sarkar's Expansion Plans
›Indienne New York is Sarkar's second restaurant.
›Plans to open more concepts at Henry Hall.
›Already operates Baar Baar in Los Angeles.
›Runs Tiya in San Francisco with his brother.
Sarkar has plans to expand further across the United States, building on a portfolio that already includes Baar Baar in Los Angeles and Tiya in San Francisco, which he runs with his brother. If the New York outpost follows Chicago's trajectory, that Michelin star may not be far behind. Reservations for Indienne New York are already in high demand. Tasting menus are available Wednesday through Sunday evenings.
